raw_case_text:
In November of 2014, a 73-year-old female with acute myeloid leukemia presented to Peking University Third Hospital (Beijing, China) with progressive nose swelling and ulceration after a severe cold. The lesions had begun two months earlier as infiltrated erythema, then rapidly increased in size and ulcerated. The patient was initially diagnosed with skin and subcutaneous infection in the nose and face (rhinofacial) and treatment with antibiotics was ineffective. Next, the lesion was diagnosed as a malignant ulcer and chemotherapy was administered, but the necrotic ulcer became progressively enlarged. Subsequent clinical diagnosis of rhinofacial mucormycosis was made and the patient was treated with AMB (initial dose 5 mg/day, increased by 5 mg daily), but the ulcer still progressed. Two months after onset of the malignant ulcer, the patient was transferred to Peking University Third Hospital.
The patient had a 1-year history of acute myeloid leukemia and had received one cycle of DA chemotherapy (daunorubicin and cytarabine), two cycles of MA chemotherapy (mitoxantrone and cytarabine), one cycle of CAG chemotherapy (cytarabine, aclarubicin, and recombinant human granulocyte-colony stimulating factor), and one cycle of AA chemotherapy (aclarubicin and cytarabine). She denied any history of preceding injury or insect bite at the site of infection. Physical examination revealed erythema, edema, and ulceration over the right nasal alae and upper lip, extending to the soft tissue around the right side of the nose (Figure 1).
A skin biopsy was performed on the lesion of the nasal dorsum. Histopathological examination later revealed inflammation, necrosis, granuloma, and angiodestruction. In addition, numerous hyaline and septate hyphae with branches at acute angles were observed throughout the dermis with angioinvasion (Figure 2). The laboratory evaluation revealed hyperleukocytosis (78.9 x 109/L), erythrocytopenia (2.44 x 1012/L), thrombocytopenia (12 x 109/L), hypokalemia (2.38 mmol/L), an elevated level of C-reactive protein (31.2 mg/dL), and a positive serum galactomannan (GM) test (1.25 mug/L). The results of the antinuclear antibody test, T cell enzyme-linked immunospot assay, and serum (1-3)-beta-d-glucan (G) test were all negative. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen and antibodies to human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis C virus, and Treponema pallidum were all negative. Leukocyte counts decreased rapidly after receiving AA chemotherapy during hospitalization (Figure 3).
Despite 7 days of continuous treatment with AMB (before biopsy), the ulcer progressed and the patient died of cerebral hemorrhage. The biopsied tissue yielded an Aspergillus isolate that was initially identified by morphology as A. flavus. However, the antifungal susceptibility profile of the culture showed resistance to AMB.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 73-year-old female with acute myeloid leukemia presented with a 2-month history of progressive right nasal and upper lip swelling, erythema, and deep necrotic ulceration following a severe cold.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior to transfer in November 2014, following a severe upper respiratory infection, the patient developed infiltrated erythema on her nose that rapidly enlarged and ulcerated. At an outside hospital, she failed empirical antibiotics for presumed bacterial cellulitis, chemotherapy for presumed malignant leukemic cutis/ulcer, and escalating intravenous amphotericin B (starting at 5 mg/day) for presumed rhinofacial mucormycosis, with relentless enlargement of the necrotic rhinofacial ulcer.
subjective.past_medical_history: 1-year history of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) treated with 1 cycle of DA (daunorubicin/cytarabine), 2 cycles of MA (mitoxantrone/cytarabine), 1 cycle of CAG (cytarabine/aclarubicin/G-CSF), and 1 cycle of AA (aclarubicin/cytarabine); denied local facial trauma or insect bites.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive painful rhinofacial erythema, edema, and necrotic ulceration.

objective.physical_examination: Marked erythema, edema, and deep necrotic ulceration involving the right nasal ala, nasal dorsum, and upper lip, extending into the right paranasal facial soft tissues.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs revealed hyperleukocytosis (WBC 78.9 x 10^9/L, which dropped rapidly after inpatient AA chemotherapy), anemia (RBC 2.44 x 10^12/L), severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 12 x 10^9/L), hypokalemia (2.38 mmol/L), and elevated CRP (31.2 mg/dL). ANA, T-cell ELISpot TB assay, HBsAg, anti-HCV, anti-HIV, and Treponema pallidum antibodies were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Serum galactomannan (GM) was positive at 1.25 ug/L, while serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (G test) was negative. Skin biopsy of the nasal dorsum ulcer demonstrated dermal inflammation, necrosis, granuloma formation, and prominent angiodestruction/angioinvasion by numerous acute-angle branching hyaline septate hyphae. Tissue culture isolated Aspergillus flavus, and in vitro antifungal susceptibility testing confirmed resistance to amphotericin B.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal primary rhinofacial cutaneous/subcutaneous invasive aspergillosis caused by amphotericin B-resistant Aspergillus flavus in a patient with relapsed/refractory AML, confirmed by positive serum galactomannan (1.25 ug/L), nasal skin biopsy histopathology showing dermal angioinvasion by acute-angle branching septate hyphae, and tissue culture and susceptibility testing. Because the lesion was initially misdiagnosed clinically as mucormycosis and treated with amphotericin B (to which the A. flavus isolate was resistant) alongside AA cytoreductive chemotherapy, the necrotic ulcer progressed and the patient died of cerebral hemorrhage before targeted azole therapy could take effect.
